This is a "Yes, but..." situation. Yes it's a cute and fun little game. You just aim your weapon over a small battle arena to slay monsters, and they drop XP to levelup your weapon skills PLUS gold to buy various upgrades in the shop's "skill tree." But... here's where the "bad stuff" comes in... It is EARLY ACCESS really. So if you're expecting a fully polished game, it's NOT DONE YET. The developer is actively working on bug fixes and QOL improvements. So maybe wait a month or two before you buy, if this situation worries you. The game "mostly works" and you can have some fun with it as-is, and he is very responsive to bug reports and questions. But it does still need some work before I'd call it "finished." DO NOT play the demo. It is a very old version, and will give you a bad impression of the full game. The full game is much improved compared to the demo. Go watch a youtube video of someone playing, instead of getting the demo. This might change later, the dev has said he will eventually make a better version of the demo but first he's worried about fixing bugs and other concerns with the full version. A lot of the special attacks and menu features don't currently have sound effects, so the game feels a bit "empty" because of that. But the dev is working on finding some appropriate sounds to add in there. The art style is VERY minimalistic. You just get a small square battle arena, with polygon-esque monsters to battle. Black void in the background, with some puffy little clouds floating across. There are two battle modes: arena, where you fight a huge mob of monsters that drop gold and XP for your weapon; and raids, where you fight a single boss monster who drops Enlightenment points. The Enlightenment skill tree is supposed to give you buffs to one skill, while debuffing another skill, for each skill you buy there. HOWEVER, currently it's broken - the debuffs are BIGGER than the buffs, so it makes you weaker to unlock these. The dev is working on rebalancing it. Raids ALSO unlock a new (stronger, probably) weapon if you defeat raid level 20. The Awakening skill tree has a lot of neat buffs. Direct stat buffs are nice, but at level 10 you also get to choose an elemental affinity for your weapon (fire, lightning, or ice). If you pick the right 2 awakening skills and max out their level, they will combine into a stronger skill! But the game doesn't (and WON'T because the dev said the mystery is intentional) tell you which two skills will combine. When you combine skills, you'll unlock a new (stronger, probably) weapon. To equip your new weapons, go back to the menu and press the "PLAY" button. Each new weapon forces you to start from the beginning again so you can build it with a new awakening skill set, and you'll need to earn gold to unlock the main upgrade tree again too. But you will keep your CHRONICLE, which gives you bonus gold based on how many enemies you've slain in total. And you also keep your WARRIOR LEVEL, which gives you a bonus to gold earned at the end of each combat. Everything else resets though. But don't panic, your progress on all of your old weapons is saved, so you can just equip them again to pick up right where you left off. You also sometimes find relics dropped by enemies, equipping 2 or more of a set will give you special bonuses. But currently these are broken - the drop rate is essentially ZERO until you reach a late-game upgrade node that boosts drop rate by 500%. The dev is currently rebalancing this, so the relic experience should be better in the next couple of update patches. And some of the skills, when maxed out, put SO MANY special effects and damage number on screen that it will lag or crash the game. Needs a bit of optimization on that front. So yeah, nice fun little game. Simplistic art style. Soundscape needs a bit of love. Bit buggy and not the best balance on some features, but the dev is working to rebalance and bugfix. It's worth a few bucks, but be aware currently it should be considered as "early access" because of all the bugs and rebalancing that need touching up.

I loved the original demo. But the direction this game took wasn't what was originally imagined. Originally it was something special. It was a slow grind and you would unlock new weapons with new abilities as you constantly progress through one playthrough with new harder levels with new harder enemies. Now the game has been stripped down to a short 30 minute arcade reset where each weapon is the same, ability selection is random from a pool of 3 and the pool of 3 doesn't ever really change much. There may be 6 total abilities that can be chosen for your playthrough but the only good choice right now is Ice. On reset you have to customly again for the 10th time fill out a pointless passive tree that should fill itself out anyway, you choose a new weapon that doesn't matter because the game is the exact same, same 20 raids, same passive skills, same abilities, same passives for the weapon. Same difficulty scaling, same enemies and levels. You get about 30 minutes to 45 minutes of active unique gameplay before the loop starts and the exact same experience is done again and again and again for absolutely nothing. The game has no point, no progression, no progress, no actual cool unique unlocks. Just the exact same experience over and over until you get bored. This has been stripped down from its original design and it is now just a lazy boring recycled loop. Nothing changes, no point in continuing or unlocking new weapons, abilities are boring and the same, no actual profile progress just a boring short arcade loop. I had high hopes for this and purchased it right after release. I have more time in the Demo than I do in the actual game. The Demo was so much better when it first came out. I don't know what happened here or why but the balance is horrible, there is no late game, some ability choices crush the game instantly and others have you struggle until the end. You just kill 20 raid bosses over and over and over. Each fight takes 2 seconds and you just click one after the other to reset to choose a weapon that does the exact same thing the one before it. I feel bad. The graphics are great, the core concept used to be there but isn't anymore, there is no point to this game, no point to the unlocks, no point for new weapons, no progress, just a short loop. It is so lazy to reset the game and force people to do the same game again over and over. What happened to the single playthrough with the infinite level and boss release progress? What happened to the weapons with thier unique abilities to fit your playstyle?

Re:Blade is an action-focused roguelike developed and published by STAGE Games that combines automated combat systems with progression-driven gameplay built around experimentation and long-term growth. Instead of emphasizing precision combos or highly technical action mechanics, the game leans heavily into strategy, build creation, and repeated runs that slowly transform an underpowered warrior into something significantly stronger. It takes familiar roguelike ideas and places progression at the center of the experience, creating a gameplay loop designed around constant improvement and discovering stronger combinations over time. The foundation of the game begins with simplicity. Players enter battle carrying little more than a weapon and the goal of surviving increasingly difficult encounters. Enemies become stronger, bosses stand in the way of advancement, and every completed run creates opportunities to improve future performance. The structure embraces repetition intentionally. Progress is not measured only by how far players advance during a single attempt but also by how effectively they build long-term strength across multiple sessions. Combat operates differently from traditional action role-playing games. Attacks occur automatically, shifting attention away from constant button execution and toward movement, positioning, and strategic decisions. Players spend more time focusing on upgrade paths, build choices, and battlefield awareness than mastering complicated attack inputs. This creates a gameplay rhythm that feels approachable while still allowing room for optimization and mechanical depth. The progression systems serve as the strongest part of the experience. Throughout gameplay, players unlock upgrades that influence weapon performance and combat behavior. Different development paths allow experimentation between playstyles, encouraging repeated attempts with new approaches rather than relying on a single dominant strategy. Some builds focus heavily on raw offensive power while others emphasize survival or specialized effects. The flexibility encourages creativity and strengthens replayability. A major feature supporting this depth comes through the Awakening system. Special cards collected during progression influence how weapons evolve, creating opportunities to reshape performance over time. The system rewards players willing to experiment and discover synergies rather than simply pursuing straightforward statistical improvement. Finding combinations that work well together creates satisfying moments where careful planning pays off in meaningful ways. Relic systems add another layer of progression complexity. Defeated enemies occasionally reward players with relic components capable of forming larger combinations when assembled properly. Completing these sets unlocks additional bonuses that can dramatically change combat effectiveness. The system creates an enjoyable balance between immediate rewards and long-term planning, encouraging players to think beyond short-term decisions. Boss encounters help reinforce progression pacing effectively. Larger enemies act as major checkpoints that test preparation and understanding of mechanics. Victories feel rewarding because progress depends not only on numerical strength but also on understanding how systems interact. These battles help maintain momentum while providing goals that consistently encourage continued improvement. The game also includes progression systems that extend beyond individual runs. Failure rarely feels wasted because advancement continues even after defeat. Resources earned through repeated attempts contribute toward future power growth, creating a sense of momentum that keeps progression satisfying over longer sessions. The design understands an important principle of roguelike structure: setbacks should motivate improvement rather than create frustration. Visually, Re:Blade favors readability and clear combat presentation over overwhelming visual complexity. Effects remain easy to follow even during larger battles, helping players focus on decision-making and positioning rather than visual noise. The fantasy presentation complements progression systems effectively while maintaining clarity during faster moments. One of the game’s strongest achievements comes from pacing. New systems appear gradually enough to remain approachable while steadily expanding complexity over time. Players are not overloaded immediately with endless mechanics. Instead, the game introduces features in ways that support learning and encourage experimentation naturally. Its more specialized structure naturally limits appeal for certain audiences. Players looking for heavily narrative-driven experiences or direct manual combat mastery may find the automated combat design less engaging than traditional action titles. Much of the satisfaction comes from optimization and progression rather than execution-heavy gameplay. The repetitive structure may also divide players unfamiliar with roguelike design philosophy. Repeated failures and gradual advancement remain central to the experience. Those who enjoy experimentation and long-term growth will likely appreciate the structure far more than players seeking purely linear progression. What ultimately allows Re:Blade to stand out is how confidently it embraces its strengths. STAGE Games builds an experience focused entirely on progression systems and player-driven experimentation without overcomplicating its foundation. The result feels focused rather than limited. For players who enjoy build optimization, repeated progression loops, and roguelike systems centered around becoming steadily stronger through persistence and experimentation, Re:Blade offers a rewarding gameplay cycle that remains engaging through refinement rather than spectacle. Rating: 6/10

Firstly, this bit right here is seriously false advertising ----> "action roguelike where every run reshapes your blade and every boss falls to your steps." It is absolutely not remotely anything like a roguelike, it is a standard basic incremental, nothing more. And the reshaping the blade bit,, seriously, that's literally all that does change when you swap from one weapon to another, every other aspect remains virtually the same. Sure awakening can be done different each time, but the result is still the same, you hover over the monster till it's dispatched, get the gold, upgrade, fill the skill tree, collect the relics, repeat. Would I recommend the game??? As an incremental, yes. It's not a bad incremental game and the price is about right for it. For using the term roguelike, absolutely not. STAGE GAMES, change your description ffs, it's not a roguelike... Anyway, so based on that, do I give the game a thumbs up or a thumbs down... So I guess I need to break it down... I got through the first playthrough in 2.4 hours. But I can see it has several other weapons to play through, should I choose to do so. I like the awakening feature, it adds a little more interest. Goblin pouches... Seriously... Over 500 chests needed just to get the goblin relics and by the end of the playthrough, I still didn't have anything like close to all of the skeleton or orc relics. Never mind any of the other ones. Do I like the incremental aspect of the game enough to go back and do more weapons... Yes. Will I do it though... Possibly, if I can't find something else I want to play. Honestly, I would likely give this game a 7 out of 10 as an incremental, if the use of the word roguelike hadn't bothered me so much. But because of it, I can only think 5 max. The deciding factor for me though, is the price. It's less than the cost of a happy meal at McDonalds and more satisfying, although I did set the bar quite low. So based on price and thinking of it as an incremental, then yes, it gets a thumbs up, but not a big thumb, just a little thumb.

This is yet another "wish there was a neutral option" review. The tags for this game are [b]entirely[/b] inaccurate. [b]This is an incremental game[/b]. It's not a Roguelike, it's not an Auto Battler, and it's only an Idler if you choose specific skill upgrades. Those tags are all very misleading - let me explain. You have a weapon which utilizes your mouse cursor. You must hover over enemies in order for the weapon to deal damage, and they move around on screen. The first time you go through the game, it's interesting as you learn how it works and try different skill and weapon combinations. However, you complete your first run in about an hour, then the second in about 20 minutes, then the third in about 5, and from there it's just pure and complete repetition. You'll have tried all sensible combinations by your 4th run, so what's really left to do? The game genuinely is expecting you to beat the same game over and over about 30 times. That is not an exaggeration, it may even be underselling it a bit. Nothing changes or gets harder - in fact it becomes so trivial that it's just a repetitive slog of spending more time choosing upgrades than actually playing the game. The skill tree even has a "upgrade for me" option because even the devs knew you wouldn't do it a second time. I played for 4 hours but I don't see any reason why I'd want to do this another 26 times. Nothing changes with each run - the weapons even all feel the same too, and once you unlock any element, the game will play and beat itself. This game left me wanting far more than what's there, but it was a decent time-killer for the little bit that I played. If you have nothing better to do, this'll do the trick, otherwise I wouldn't recommend.
